title: A Prime Agent decides whether to deploy an Integration Boost by weighing its Distribution Reward earnings against the cost of funding the boost
content:
A.2.2.9.2.2.3.1.2 sets out the first step of an Integration Boost Invocation as a calculation, not an aspiration: "The Prime Agent identifies a DeFi protocol or market where an Integration Boost would drive adoption. The Prime Agent estimates the potential earnings from the Distribution Reward associated with the incremental USDS usage **versus** the operational cost of funding the Sky Savings Rate payouts."

The two sides of that comparison are the two Primitives the Prime holds. Revenue comes from the Distribution Reward on the additional USDS the integration attracts; cost is the Savings-Rate-equivalent payout the Boost delivers. The Prime Agent is therefore acting as an investor deciding whether an integration clears its own hurdle rate, and the second planning step — negotiating cadence and how much Distribution Reward to share with the partner (A.2.2.9.2.2.1.4.3) — is the price negotiation that follows.

The design consequence is decentralized capital allocation over demand generation. Sky does not maintain a list of protocols worth subsidizing; it defines the reward and cost structures and lets Prime Agents locate the profitable integrations. Poor targets are filtered by the Prime's own arithmetic rather than by a central reviewer.

The corresponding bias is toward integrations with measurable, near-term balance growth. An integration with strategic value but weak attributable volume fails the Prime's test even where the ecosystem might want it, because the Prime bears the funding cost and captures only the Distribution Reward on what it can attribute.
description: The planning step is an explicit profitability test on incremental USDS usage, so Prime Agents self-select which integrations are worth subsidizing rather than following a central allocation.
